rv.q: Despite handsome design elements and a score with pleasing melodies, this ambitious musical adaptation of Dickens' classic novel suffers from a bloated book that fails to dramatize effectively.

This stolid poperetta, which features book, music and lyrics by Jill Santoriello and is directed and choreographed by Warren Carlyle, is one of those unfortunate shows that are neither witty in themselves nor able to inspire wit in others.
And in much better crafted company?
From the moment the first chords are struck, you may get the sense you've heard it all before.
Despite a soaring score by Jill Santoriello that represents the best aspect of this misguided effort, the show suffers from a bewildering book
It has lots of nice period costumes and good actors singing their lungs inside out.
Barbour is the best asset of this otherwise awful musical.

They haven't, but first-time composer-lyricist-librettist Jill Santoriello and her colleagues still needed to do something radical to raise their blatant attempt at cloning Les Miserables above the level of Anglo-Gallic mediocrity that now appears on the stage of the Theatre.
The entertaining evening unfortunately lacks inspiration.
